text: Tantalum is a chemical element with the symbol Ta and atomic number 73, named after the Greek mythological figure Tantalus. It is a hard, ductile, lustrous, blue-gray transition metal known for its high corrosion resistance and extremely high melting point of 3017 °C (boiling point 5458 °C), which is exceeded only by tungsten, rhenium, osmium, and carbon among metals. Tantalum is part of group 5, along with vanadium and niobium, and is always found in nature together with niobium in mineral groups such as tantalite, columbite, and coltan. It is chemically inert and highly resistant to acids, especially aqua regia at temperatures below 150 °C, though it can be dissolved by hydrofluoric acid or acidic solutions containing fluoride ions and sulfur trioxide, as well as molten potassium hydroxide. Tantalum exists in two crystalline phases: the alpha phase, which is stable up to the melting point and has a body-centered cubic structure with lattice constant a = 0.33029 nm at 20 °C, and the beta phase, which is hard, brittle, tetragonal, and metastable, converting to the alpha phase upon heating to 750–775 °C. Bulk tantalum is mostly alpha phase, while the beta phase is typically produced as thin films via magnetron sputtering, chemical vapor deposition, or electrochemical deposition. Natural tantalum consists of two stable isotopes: 180mTa (0.012%) and 181Ta (99.988%), with 180mTa being a metastable isomer predicted to decay via isomeric transition, beta decay, or electron capture, though its radioactivity has never been observed and only a lower limit of 2.9×10¹⁷ years on its half-life has been established; the ground state of 180Ta has a half-life of 8 hours. Tantalum forms compounds in oxidation states from −3 to +5, with Ta(V) oxides being the most common, and it is barely soluble in dilute hydrochloric, sulfuric, nitric, or phosphoric acids due to precipitation of hydrous Ta(V) oxide, but can be solubilized in basic media via polyoxotantalate species. Tantalum pentoxide (Ta₂O₅) is the most important compound for applications. Tantalates, such as lithium tantalate (LiTaO₃) and lanthanum tantalate (LaTaO₄), are well-known compounds. The hardest known compounds of tantalum are its nitrides and carbides; tantalum carbide (TaC) is used in cutting tools, and tantalum(III) nitride is used as a thin film insulator in microelectronics. Tantalum sulfide (TaS₂) is a layered semiconductor, and a tantalum-tellurium alloy forms quasicrystals. Tantalum halides include TaF₅ (melting point 97.0 °C), [TaF₇]²⁻ (used for separation from niobium), and TaCl₅ (a dimer that hydrolyzes readily), with lower halides TaX₄ and TaX₃ featuring Ta-Ta bonds. Organotantalum compounds include pentamethyltantalum, mixed alkyltantalum chlorides, alkyltantalum hydrides, alkylidene complexes, and cyclopentadienyl derivatives, as well as salts and substituted derivatives of hexacarbonyl [Ta(CO)₆]⁻ and related isocyanides. Tantalum is estimated to make up about 1–2 ppm of the Earth's crust. Key tantalum minerals include tantalite (Fe, Mn)Ta₂O₆, which is the most important for extraction, microlite, wodginite, euxenite (euxenite-(Y)), polycrase (polycrase-(Y)), samarskite, and fergusonite; tantalite and columbite have the same structure, with tantalite containing more tantalum and columbite more niobium. Gravitational separation is used due to the high density of these minerals. Australia was the main producer of tantalum before the 2010s, with Global Advanced Metals (formerly Talison Minerals) operating mines at Greenbushes and Wodgina in Western Australia; the Wodgina mine reopened in January 2011 after being suspended in 2008 due to the financial crisis, but operations ceased in February 2012 due to softening demand. Wodgina produces a primary tantalum concentrate upgraded at Greenbushes. While Brazil and Canada are major niobium producers, their ores also contain small amounts of tantalum. China, Ethiopia, Mozambique, Thailand, and Malaysia mine ores with higher tantalum content, with Thailand and Malaysia producing tantalum as a by-product of tin mining, where tantalite is found in placer deposits and recovered from tin smelter slag. Since the start of the 21st century, tantalum production has shifted significantly from Australia and Brazil to the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Rwanda, and other African countries, with Congo producing nearly 40% and Rwanda and Burundi contributing about 18% of global production by 2021. Tantalum is considered a conflict resource because coltan, the mineral from which it is extracted, is found in Central Africa and has been linked to conflict in the DRC, where smuggling of coltan has contributed to war resulting in approximately 5.4 million deaths since 1998, making it one of the world's deadliest conflicts since WWII. Ethical concerns arise over corporate responsibility, human rights, and environmental damage in conflict zones. The United States Geological Survey reported that the DRC produced less than 1% of global tantalum output from 2002–2006, peaking at 10% in 2000 and 2008. Extraction begins with crushing and gravity separation of the ore, followed by leaching with hydrofluoric acid and sulfuric or hydrochloric acid to separate tantalum and niobium from impurities. The resulting fluoride complexes are separated via liquid-liquid extraction into organic solvents like cyclohexanone, octanol, or methyl isobutyl ketone, removing impurities. Niobium is then separated by lowering ionic strength, forming oxyfluoride H₂[NbOF₅], while purified H₂[TaF₇] is neutralized with ammonia to precipitate hydrated tantalum oxide, which is calcined to Ta₂O₅. Alternatively, H₂[TaF₇] can be treated with potassium fluoride to form K₂[TaF₇], which is easily crystallized and reduced to metallic tantalum using sodium at approximately 800 °C in molten salt. The older Marignac process involves converting the mixture to K₂[TaF₇] and K₂[NbOF₅] and separating them by fractional crystallization based on water solubility. Tantalum can also be refined by electrolysis using a modified Hall–Héroult process, where powdered metal oxides are reduced in a molten salt bath with a carbon anode and a powdered oxide cathode, first demonstrated in 1997 by Cambridge University researchers.

H2[TaF7] can be treated with potassium fluoride to produce potassium heptafluorotantalate (K2[TaF7]), which is readily crystallized and handled as a solid. K2[TaF7] can be converted to metallic tantalum through reduction with sodium at approximately 800 °C in molten salt. In the older Marignac process, a mixture of H2[TaF7] and H2[NbOF5] is converted to a mixture of K2[TaF7] and K2[NbOF5], which is separated by fractional crystallization based on their differing water solubilities. Tantalum can also be refined by electrolysis using a modified Hall–Héroult process that operates on non-liquid powdered oxides; this method was first discovered in 1997 by Cambridge University researchers who immersed oxide samples in molten salt baths and reduced them with electric current. In this process, the cathode uses powdered metal oxide, the anode is carbon, and the molten salt at 1,000 °C (1,830 °F) serves as the electrolyte. The first refinery using this method has enough capacity to supply 3–4% of annual global demand. All welding of tantalum must be performed in an inert atmosphere of argon or helium to prevent contamination, and tantalum is not solderable; grinding is difficult, especially for annealed tantalum, which is extremely ductile and can be readily formed into metal sheets. The primary use of tantalum metal powder is in electronic components, especially capacitors and some high-power resistors. Tantalum electrolytic capacitors use tantalum powder pressed into a pellet as one plate, the oxide layer as the dielectric, and an electrolytic solution or conductive solid as the other plate. Because the dielectric layer can be thinner than in aluminum capacitors, high capacitance is achieved in a small volume, making tantalum capacitors ideal for portable telephones, personal computers, automotive electronics, and cameras. Tantalum is also used in alloys with high melting points, strength, and ductility, including carbide tools for metalworking and superalloys for jet engine components, chemical process equipment, nuclear reactors, missile parts, heat exchangers, tanks, and vessels. Due to its ductility, tantalum can be drawn into fine wires or filaments for evaporating metals like aluminium. Tantalum is inert to most acids except hydrofluoric acid and hot sulfuric acid, and hot alkaline solutions cause corrosion, making it suitable for chemical reaction vessels and pipes for corrosive liquids, including heat-exchanging coils for steam heating of hydrochloric acid. Historically, tantalum was used in ultra high frequency electron tubes for radio transmitters, where its ability to form oxides and nitrides helped maintain high vacuum in internal parts such as grids and plates. In surgery, tantalum is valued for its hardness, ductility, and use in sharp instruments and monofilament sutures; additionally, its unique ability to form a durable bond with human hard tissue makes it ideal for bone and dental implants. Tantalum coatings are increasingly used in complex titanium surgical implants due to their strong, biologically stable bond with hard tissue. Because tantalum is non-ferrous and non-magnetic, implants are acceptable for MRI procedures. NASA used tantalum to shield spacecraft components such as Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 from radiation. Its high melting point and oxidation resistance make it suitable for vacuum furnace parts and corrosion-resistant components like thermowells, valve bodies, and fasteners. Due to its high density, tantalum is used in shaped charge and explosively formed penetrator liners, enhancing armor penetration capabilities. It is also occasionally used in precious watches, such as those by Audemars Piguet, F. P. Journe, Hublot, Montblanc, Omega, and Panerai. Tantalum oxide is used to produce special high refractive index glass for camera lenses. Spherical tantalum powder, produced by atomizing molten tantalum with gas or liquid, is commonly used in additive manufacturing due to its uniform shape, excellent flowability, and high melting point. Tantalum receives little attention in environmental studies; upper crust concentration (UCC) is 0.92 ppm and the Nb/Ta(w/w) ratio is 12.7. Reliable data on tantalum concentrations in natural waters are lacking, with dissolved concentrations in seawater and freshwaters not reliably measured and likely below 1 ng L−1 due to analytical limitations. Tantalum appears mostly as particulate matter in natural waters. Soil concentrations are near 1 ppm, indicating a detrital origin; atmospheric aerosol values are scattered and limited, with enrichment likely due to loss of more water-soluble elements in clouds. No pollution linked to human use has been detected, and tantalum is considered a very conservative element in biogeochemical terms, though its cycling and reactivity are not fully understood. Tantalum compounds are rarely encountered in the laboratory; the metal is highly biocompatible and used in body implants and coatings, so focus may be on other elements or the physical properties of the compounds. Workplace exposure to tantalum can occur through inhalation, skin contact, or eye contact. OSHA sets the permissible exposure limit at 5 mg/m³ over an 8-hour workday, and NIOSH recommends a 5 mg/m³ limit over 8 hours and a short-term limit of 10 mg/m³. A paradox exists because tantalum's strong bonding to bone tissue means that at 2500 mg/m³, tantalum dust becomes immediately dangerous to life and health if it bonds with incorrect tissues.
